To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the Lounesto classification can be built (defined) upon two spinor arrangement, and that such arrangement can be split into two parts, which are not necessarily related to the Lounesto class, and that the arrangement does not necessarily inherit such characteristics.

(a) The Lounesto’s spinor classification is based upon two spinors arrangements; (b) Each part of such arrangements may be classified in distinct sectors; (c) Such arrangement can be used to unveil the hidden characteristics of the spinor, which can not be seen directly.
the Lounesto classification is not a complete classification of spinors and the spinor arrangement is a non-trivial process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the spinor arrangement and how this can be applied to the Lounesto spinor classification.
the study of the spinor arrangement and how the resulting spinors can be classified according to the Lounesto classification.
how the Lounesto classification can be built upon two spinors arrangements.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Lounesto classification is not a spinor invariant.
the Lounesto classification of spinors is a very useful tool to investigate and understand the spinor’s behaviour, but it does not provide an absolute classification.
the Lounesto classification does not necessarily preserve the class and the dynamic properties of the spinors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Lounesto classification can be seen as a tool that allow us to better understand spinors and their physical properties.

the Lounesto classification is not invariant under spinor arrangements, which can be seen as a consequence of the fact that the spinors are defined by their components, which are not invariant under spinors arrangement.

the arrangement of spinors belonging to a specific class does not necessarily result in a spinor belonging to the same class, as example, we show that the arrangement of a pair of spinors belonging both to the regular and the singular sectors of the classification, does not result in a regular or a singular spinor, but a regular and singular spinor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Lounesto classification is not a rigid one, and it is possible to build (or define) a new spinor belonging to a distinct class, from the arrangement of spinors belonging to a different class.
the spinor arrangement does not necessarily preserve the characteristics of the composing spinors.

, in general, the resulting spinors from the arrangement of spinors (belonig to a distinct class) does not necessarily belong to the same class of the spinors which compose them, and the same applies to the physical information encoded into the resulting spinor, as we shall see.
